William Carpenter, London A George III ormolu, enamel and paste-set jewellery cabinet with music and astronomical paste-set pair-cased watch with visible balance and seed pearl and ceramic bead decorated enamel scene of a windmill, signed William Carpenter no. 4647, Made for the Chinese Market, Circa 1790 and later Case: The cabinet with two tiers set with neo-classical ornament, the lower section with concave corners and padded silk lined drawer, the upper section with a mirrored-pair of polychrome enamel oval scene of figures within coloured paste-set bezels to the doors, inside with 10 padded silk lined drawers with deep blue guilloche enamel fronts, each with a paste-set ribbon bow pull, the deeper central drawer with drop-in tray over a concealed compartment, the plinth with a later 19 th music box, surmounted by a later watch stand with paired peacocks over a gimballed double sided cheval glass with coloured paste-set bezels Size: 500 mm high x 280 mm deep Provenance: Baron Mayer Amschel de Rothschild, Mentmore, Buckinghamshire, his daughter, Hannah de Rothschild, Countess of Rosebery, Mentmore Works of Art and Silver, Sothebys Parke Bernet & Co, sold on behalf of the Estate of the late 6 th Earl Of Rosebery and his family, May 23 rd 1977, Lot 1815, Asprey & Gerard London The 1930s was the golden age of country house sales. British society was going through a seismic shift in the wake of the First World War. Many of the vast estates became untenable to fund for the families who had lived there for centuries. SothebyÃ¢ÂÂs staged some twenty on-site auctions at various country houses during the 1930s (there were seven in one year alone). Specialists uncovered a treasure trove of items during their time on the road. Those early days of fast-turnaround auctions created the foundations for the grand events to follow, such as SothebyÃ¢ÂÂs 1977 landmark sale at Mentmore Towers in Buckinghamshire where the present lot was fully illustrated and sold. The Sotheby's Mentmore sale in May 1977 was a landmark auction of the contents of the Rothschild estate, Mentmore Towers. The sale included almost 3,000 lots from the house and grounds, with a focus on 18th and 19th-century items, such as furniture, works of art, porcelain, silver, and paintings. At the end of the 18 th century European horologists and craftsmen from other associated trades, dealing through London, were collaborating to produce fabulous clocks and watches with entertaining complications, in the hope that they would appeal to their wealthy Chinese clients. For over one hundred years the trade in silks, fine porcelains and tea had grown to such an extent that it became necessary to attempt to correct the trade imbalance. The Chinese considered that there was very little produced in Europe that they were unable to obtain within their own economy, but their enthusiasm for highly decorative and novelty watches and clocks made in or sold through London provided an opportunity for trade. Since the end of the 17 th century, London had gained a worldwide reputation for horological innovation and accuracy of timekeeping. However, the restrained characteristics of traditional English clock making did not satisfy Chinese tastes and it was necessary for English merchants to use the best Europe-wide resources available to them in order to appeal. As trade in these novelties was established, the demand for ever-more complicated and decorative clocks grew and the Qing Emperors became some of the most important collectors. The present lot is very unusual and would have been very sought-after by Chinese collectors of this period. Like many other Western objects, once they reached the Qianlong Emperor they were then customized by his many clockmakers based in the palace. A music box was fitted to the plinth later and the stand connected to the mirror to support the watch was also applied later of the making of the cabinet itself.

He specialized in the production of larger size watches, made specifically for the Chinese Market. During the Qianlong EmperorÃ¢ÂÂs reign (1736-1795), Western timepieces were extremely popular, not only were they collected by the Imperial Palace, but they were also purchased and treasured by higher officials, rich merchants and scholars.
